title: Concerning a Civil Principality
coreMove: Build civil power on the side whose demand can be satisfied without making equals into rivals.
sourcePressure: The chapter explains civil principalities, where a leading citizen becomes prince through the people or the nobles. Nobles want to rule and oppress and see themselves as equals; the people mainly want not to be oppressed. Popular foundations are safer in adversity, but a prince must keep citizens needing the state and him, not only promising loyalty in quiet times.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version writes about popularity, democracy, or class politics in general. The writer must keep the strategic test: nobles are few but dangerous rivals, people are many and cannot be secured against if hostile, and quiet-time promises do not prove adversity loyalty.

counterintuition: most people assume elites are safer, but actually the people are better
popular support solves every legitimacy problem
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds and ask who likes you
examples: corporate middle manager pleasing executives and staff

exampleSpecs.domain: a grain-market magistrate elevated after mill owners and bakers clash over famine prices
exampleSpecs.audience: a leading citizen deciding whether to owe office to mill owners or to market crowds
exampleSpecs.stakes: mill owners want freedom to squeeze, while the crowd wants bread not to be taken from them; one demand can be satisfied without empowering equals
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: He moves the mill owners' private price slate away from the public loaf scale and posts the anti-seizure order where the crowd can see it.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A public loaf scale stands beside a private mill owners' price slate.

exampleSpecs.domain: a harbor pilot elected protector after shipowners try to control all berth assignments
exampleSpecs.audience: a civic leader who rose because crews and fishers feared being squeezed by shipowners
exampleSpecs.stakes: shipowners can conspire with money and captains, while ordinary crews only ask not to lose berths and wages
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: She refuses the shipowners' velvet berth book, writes crew appeal hours on a tide board, and makes the first order protect access rather than reward the men who offered her office.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A velvet berth book lies closed beside a chalked tide board.

exampleSpecs.domain: a hill-town militia captain made ruler by noble houses during a peasant tax revolt
exampleSpecs.audience: a captain who owes his title to nobles but must win the people before adversity
exampleSpecs.stakes: the noble houses see him as their equal and instrument, while villagers expected punishment and can become devoted if protected from extra levies
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: After accepting the nobles' silver baton, he breaks the extra levy tablets in the square and orders the tax clerks to read the protection decree aloud.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A silver baton rests across a stack of extra levy tablets.

exampleSpecs.domain: a market-city judge studying which noble allies bind themselves to his fortune before a siege scare
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince sorting nobles who are loyal, timid, useful for counsel, or ambitious enemies
exampleSpecs.stakes: in prosperity all nobles promise support; in adversity, ambitious ones will save themselves by opening talks with the expected winner
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The judge places each noble's pledge token on one of two boards: bound to our danger or keeping a second door open, then changes who receives command keys.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Pledge tokens sit between two boards under an unlit siege lantern.

exampleSpecs.domain: a river city transitioning from magistrate rule to direct command during flood defense
exampleSpecs.audience: a civil prince learning that people used to magistrate orders may not obey him in tumults
exampleSpecs.stakes: quiet-time applause means little if flood crews still look to magistrates while the embankment fails
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: He calls for sand crews from the balcony, then sees everyone wait for the magistrates' drum before moving, proving his authority has not passed through the old channel.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A magistrates' drum hangs above stacked flood sand sacks.

exampleSpecs.domain: a textile city where guild workers raised a dyer to block merchant-house domination
exampleSpecs.audience: a new civil prince deciding whether to keep the people needing the state and him
exampleSpecs.stakes: workers can abandon him in adversity unless the dye-house courts, wage measures, and guard rotations make protection a daily dependence
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: When the merchant houses offer a banquet seat, he keeps his stained measuring rod on the wage court table and asks which order prevents oppression tomorrow morning.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A stained measuring rod lies across a wage court table.

skillTargets: distinguish civil principality from conquest, wicked seizure, or hereditary rule
identify whether nobles or people raised the ruler and what each side wants
analyze which nobles bind themselves, hang back from timidity, or pursue their own ambition
evaluate whether popular support will endure adversity because people need the state and prince, not because they promised loyalty in quiet times

tryThisNowSpec: Pick a leader raised by internal factions rather than conquest. Write who elevated them, what that group wants, whether the people are protected from oppression, and what would be tested first in adversity.
